title: TINNs: Time-Induced Neural Networks for Solving Time-Dependent PDEs
claim: Standard models feed time as just another input to shared weights; ours moves time into the parameters, so weights evolve with time.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, divider line, ours boxed in red
description: Two side-by-side panels separated by a vertical line. The left panel, titled 'Vanilla Neural Network u_θ(x,t)', shows a fully connected network with black edges. A blue box holds the spatial input x and a small red box holds the temporal input t, and both feed the same first layer. A single θ label marks the shared weights. The right panel is enclosed in a red rounded rectangle and titled 'Time-Induced Neural Network u_θ(t)(x)'. It shows the same network drawn with red edges. Only the blue spatial input x enters the first layer, and a red 'Temporal Input θ(t)' label marks the weights as functions of time. Blue and red color coding separates space from time, and the red frame draws the eye to the proposed method.
caption: Space–time PINN (time as input) vs. TINN (time in parameter space). The left shows how a vanilla neural network structure deals with time-dependent PDEs. The time is incorporated into the input dimension. On the right-hand side, the time information in TINN is integrated into the parameter space, making it easier to capture the complex dynamics of the system.
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) by learning a mesh-free, differentiable solution that can be evaluated anywhere in space and time. However, standard space-time PINNs take time as an input but reuse a single network with shared weights across all times, forcing the same features to represent markedly different dynamics. This coupling degrades error performance and can destabilize training when enforcing PDE, boundary, and initial constraints jointly. We propose Time-Induced Neural Networks (TINNs), a novel architecture that parameterizes the network weights as a learned function of time, allowing the effective spatial representation to evolve over time while maintaining shared structure. The resulting formulation naturally yields a nonlinear least-squares problem, which we optimize efficiently using a Levenberg-Marquardt method. Experiments on various time-dependent PDEs show up to 4 times improved relative error and 10 times faster convergence compared to PINNs and strong baselines.
